t: Zeroth and First Law of Thermodynamics
def: The zeroth law states that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other, defining temperature. The first law states that heat supplied to a system equals the increase in its internal energy plus the work done by it.
points: Zeroth law lets us use a thermometer: all bodies at the same temperature are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
First law is energy conservation applied to heat: dQ = dU + dW.
dQ is heat supplied to the system, dU is change in internal energy, dW is work done BY the system.
Sign convention: heat absorbed is positive, heat given out is negative; work done by the gas is positive, work done on the gas is negative.
Internal energy U depends only on temperature for an ideal gas, not on the path taken.
The first law is simply the law of conservation of energy applied to thermodynamic processes.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Heat supplied dQ"] --> B["Splits into two parts"]
  B --> C["Increase in internal energy dU"]
  B --> D["Work done by system dW"]

example: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on surroundings. By first law, dU = dQ - dW = 500 - 200 = 300 J increase in internal energy.
tip: Always state the sign convention before substituting numbers — half the marks in first-law numericals are for correct signs.

def: An isothermal process occurs at constant temperature, so internal energy does not change. An adiabatic process occurs with no heat exchange with surroundings.
points: Isothermal: T is constant, so dU = 0; by first law, dQ = dW — all heat supplied converts to work.
For an ideal gas undergoing isothermal change, PV = constant (Boyle's law applies).
Work done in isothermal process: W = nRT ln(V2/V1).
Adiabatic: dQ = 0 (well-insulated system or very fast process); by first law, dU = -dW.
For adiabatic process, PV^γ = constant, where γ = Cp/Cv.
In adiabatic expansion the gas does work using its own internal energy, so its temperature falls; in adiabatic compression, temperature rises.
formula: Isothermal: PV = constant, W = nRT ln(V2/V1)     Adiabatic: PV^γ = constant, dU = −dW

diagram.draw: Draw a P-V graph with two curves starting from the same point: label the gentler curve 'isothermal (PV=const)' and the steeper, more sharply falling curve 'adiabatic (PV^gamma=const)'. Mark axes P (pressure) vertical and V (volume) horizontal.

example: 1 mole of gas expands isothermally at 300 K from 2 L to 4 L: W = nRT ln(V2/V1) = 1 x 8.314 x 300 x ln(2) = 1729 J.
tip: On the P-V diagram the adiabatic curve is always steeper than the isothermal curve at any common point — markers check this.

def: Thermodynamic work done by a gas during expansion or compression equals the area under the pressure-volume (P-V) curve for that process.
points: For a small change in volume dV at pressure P, small work done dW = P dV.
Total work for a finite change = integral of P dV from initial to final volume.
On a P-V graph, this integral equals the area under the curve between the two volumes.
If volume increases (expansion), work done by gas is positive; if volume decreases (compression), work done by gas is negative.
The work done depends on the path taken (process), not just the initial and final states — unlike internal energy.
In a cyclic process, net work done equals the area enclosed by the closed loop on the P-V diagram.
formula: W = ∫ P dV  (= area under the P-V curve)

diagram.draw: Draw a P-V diagram with a curve going from point A (P1,V1) to point B (P2,V2). Shade the region below the curve down to the V-axis between V1 and V2, and label it 'work done = shaded area'.

example: Gas at constant pressure 2 x 10^5 Pa expands from 1 L to 3 L: W = P(V2-V1) = 2e5 x 2e-3 = 400 J.
tip: For a cyclic process, remember the enclosed loop area (not the area under one curve) gives the net work — a frequently tested distinction.

def: A heat engine is a device that converts part of the heat absorbed from a hot reservoir into useful work, rejecting the rest to a cold reservoir. A refrigerator does the reverse — it removes heat from a cold body using external work.
points: A heat engine works in a cycle: absorbs heat Q1 from a hot source, does work W, and rejects heat Q2 to a cold sink.
By energy conservation, Q1 = W + Q2, so W = Q1 - Q2.
Efficiency of a heat engine η = W/Q1 = 1 - Q2/Q1.
A refrigerator takes heat Q2 from a cold body, work W is done on it by a compressor, and it rejects heat Q1 = W + Q2 to the hot surroundings.
Coefficient of performance (COP) of refrigerator = Q2/W = Q2/(Q1 - Q2).
No real engine can have 100% efficiency — some heat must always be rejected (second law of thermodynamics).

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Hot reservoir at T1"] -->|Q1 absorbed| B["Heat engine"]
  B -->|Work W done| C["Output work"]
  B -->|Q2 rejected| D["Cold reservoir at T2"]

example: An engine absorbs 800 J and rejects 500 J: W = 800-500 = 300 J, efficiency = 300/800 = 0.375 or 37.5%.
tip: Draw the energy-flow block diagram with arrows for Q1 in, W out, Q2 out — this diagram alone often fetches 1 mark.

def: The second law of thermodynamics states that heat cannot be completely converted into work in a cyclic process without some heat being rejected to a cold reservoir. The Carnot cycle is an ideal, reversible cycle that gives the maximum possible efficiency between two given temperatures.
points: Second law (Kelvin-Planck statement): no engine can work in a cycle and convert all absorbed heat into work.
The Carnot cycle consists of 4 steps: isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression, adiabatic compression.
It operates between two fixed temperatures T1 (hot source) and T2 (cold sink).
Because it is fully reversible with no friction or heat loss, it has the maximum possible efficiency for those two temperatures.
No real engine can exceed Carnot efficiency, since real engines have friction, so they are irreversible.
The Carnot engine is a theoretical ideal used as a benchmark to judge real engines.

diagram.draw: Draw a closed loop on a P-V diagram with 4 curved segments labelled in order: 1-2 isothermal expansion (at T1), 2-3 adiabatic expansion, 3-4 isothermal compression (at T2), 4-1 adiabatic compression. Arrows show the cycle direction.

example: A Carnot engine between 600 K and 300 K: η = 1 - 300/600 = 0.5 or 50% — the maximum possible for these two temperatures.
tip: Name the four steps of the Carnot cycle in the correct order with the correct process type (isothermal/adiabatic) — this sequence is often asked directly.

def: Efficiency of a heat engine is the fraction of absorbed heat converted to useful work. Coefficient of performance (COP) of a refrigerator is the ratio of heat removed from the cold body to the work done on it.
points: Efficiency η = W/Q1 = (Q1 - Q2)/Q1 = 1 - Q2/Q1, always less than 1 (less than 100%).
For a Carnot engine, η = 1 - T2/T1, where T1, T2 are absolute temperatures of hot and cold reservoirs.
COP = Q2/W = Q2/(Q1 - Q2), can be greater than 1 (refrigerators can remove more heat than the work put in).
For a Carnot refrigerator, COP = T2/(T1 - T2).
Higher temperature difference between reservoirs reduces engine efficiency's practical limit... actually increases efficiency but reduces COP of refrigerator.
These formulas let us compare real engines/refrigerators against the ideal Carnot limit.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Hot T1, Cold T2"] --> B["Heat engine: eta = 1 minus T2 over T1"]
  A --> C["Refrigerator: COP = T2 over T1 minus T2"]

example: A refrigerator maintains 263 K (−10°C) inside while room is at 303 K: COP = 263/(303-263) = 263/40 = 6.575.
tip: Do not confuse the two formulas — efficiency uses (T1-T2)/T1, while COP uses T2/(T1-T2). Write the reservoir temperatures in Kelvin, not Celsius.
